clue.text: What the optimist with only one suit has to do with it on Sunday (five words)

definitions.text: What the optimist with only one suit has to do with it on Sunday

parts.words: What the optimist with only one suit has to do with it on Sunday
parts.note: a man owning a single suit must wear that same suit as his Sunday best, cheerfully accepting what he has

explanation.surface: A cheerful man who owns just one suit decides what to wear to church.
explanation.walkthrough: The pun is on 'Sunday best': with only one suit, it must serve as the best, so the optimist puts on a brave face and wears it.
explanation.definitionFit: To accept a poor situation cheerfully and get as much from it as possible is the optimist's attitude.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'A very stone (8)': a word appears to be missing between 'very' and 'stone', and no scan or reprint supplies it.

definitions.meaning: ... weight is the traditional system for weighing precious metals and gems
Sergeant ... is the dashing soldier in Thomas Hardy's novel Far from the Madding Crowd

explanation.surface: A question about how heavy a particular army sergeant is.
explanation.definitionFit: Troy is a system of weights for gold and silver, and also the surname of Hardy's seductive sergeant.

clue.text: A Tennyson character out of the forest

definitions.text: A Tennyson character out of the forest

parts.words: A Tennyson character out of the forest
parts.note: Tennyson's poem about a shipwrecked sailor names its hero by a first name followed by Arden, which is also the name of a forest

explanation.surface: A figure from Tennyson's poetry emerges from among the trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of the forest' reads as a character coming out of the woods, but it means his surname is Arden, as in Shakespeare's Forest of Arden.
explanation.definitionFit: The hero of Tennyson's narrative poem 'Enoch Arden' carries this first name.

definitions.meaning: the regular beats a clock's mechanism makes
small blood-sucking arachnids that attach to animals

explanation.surface: Mechanical bugs that feed on their hosts.
explanation.definitionFit: A clock's mechanism makes regular clicking beats, and these are also the name of blood-feeding mites.

parts.note: a plain definition: openly disregards a rule or person, showing scorn

explanation.surface: Someone shows open scorn for another.
explanation.walkthrough: This early Times clue is a straight definition with no wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To flout a rule or person is to disregard it openly and scornfully.

parts.note: a shepherd folds, or pens, his sheep, and his tool is a hooked staff, so folding is done by a hooked implement

explanation.surface: A technique for folding paper or cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Folding' looks like creasing paper; it is penning sheep in a fold, where a shepherd uses his crook.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means by any means available, fair or foul, and its crook is a shepherd's staff.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'An 11 conveyance returns (7)': the wordplay is CAB reversed plus CHIC (11-across), but no clue word defines the answer, so the definition appears lost.

parts.note: a top dog is a chief cur; swap the two words and say them and you get a cloth worn on the head, at the top

explanation.surface: A two-word question asking who is the top dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top dog' suggests the leader; read as 'cur chief' backwards, the two words sound like a headscarf, which is worn on top.
explanation.definitionFit: A square of cloth worn over the head or round the neck is a covering for the top of a person.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'See 25 (3)': only a cross-reference; 25-across uses this light as a piece of its wordplay, and the entry has no clue of its own.
Clue held as 'Bird lacking knowledge (4)': CHICK less K gives the letters, but no clue word defines the answer (and K for knowledge is unexplained), so the clue appears incomplete.

parts.note: in Hamlet, the prince compares his dead father to his uncle as 'Hyperion to a' goat-legged woodland creature

explanation.surface: Something judged poorly beside the sun god Hyperion.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue quotes Hamlet's line 'So excellent a king, that was to this Hyperion to a satyr', contrasting his father with Claudius.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet sets the god Hyperion against this lustful half-goat woodland spirit of Greek myth.

clue.text: . and grey Had, in her sober livery, all things clad " (Milton)

definitions.text: . and grey Had, in her sober livery, all things clad " (Milton)

parts.words: . and grey Had, in her sober livery, all things clad " (Milton)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Paradise Lost Book IV: 'Now came still evening on, and ___ grey had in her sober livery all things clad'

explanation.surface: A line of Milton describing dusk dressing the world in grey.
explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is the dim light between sunset and night, in Paradise Lost Book IV.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton's dusk, the half-light after sunset, is personified as clothing everything in grey.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Act I and Act II (4)': DO + DO gives the letters, but no clue word defines the extinct bird, so the definition appears lost.

clue.text: Question that may give one pause (three words)

definitions.text: Question that may give one pause

parts.words: Question that may give one pause
parts.note: a sentry's challenge, which makes anyone approaching stop in their tracks

explanation.surface: A question that makes someone stop and think.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give one pause' means make one hesitate, but here it means literally halt: the sentry's challenge stops you.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the sentry's challenge to anyone approaching a guarded post, demanding identification.

parts.note: the word for secret, furtive action begins with a verb meaning thieve and ends with TH, the word 'the' without its last letter

explanation.surface: A thief-like quality found in the final item.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for furtiveness starts with STEAL, the thievish part, and ends in TH.
explanation.definitionFit: Secret, furtive movement is how a thief proceeds, unseen and unheard.

parts.note: a plain definition: existing in fact, not imagined

explanation.definitionFit: Something genuine exists in fact rather than in imagination.

parts.note: read as 'a verse in a quart': a stanza, with the letters of 'in a quart' rearranged giving the word for a four-line stanza

explanation.surface: Someone reluctant inside a quart pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Averse' is 'a verse', the definition; the letters of IN A QUART, rearranged, give the four-line stanza, with no anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A stanza of four lines is a verse, and its name echoes the four of 'quart'.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Nora met uncle (anag.) (12)': an anagram of NORA MET UNCLE, but no clue word defines the answer, so no definition can be given.
Clue held as 'The Tweed is rising (6)': HARRIS (a tweed) written upwards gives the letters, but no clue word defines the answer, so no definition can be given.

parts.note: a word for stern sounds like the surname of two German brothers famous for collecting fairy tales

explanation.surface: Writing described as a severe profession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stern' is GRIM, and the Brothers Grimm were famous authors of fairy tales, so their surname is a stern name for authorship.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm published the celebrated collection of German folk tales.

definitions.note: a noun in the clue for a verb meaning grieve; the clue's surface uses the act of lamenting

indicators.note: the word signals that the letters of the phrase before it produce, by rearrangement, the word after

explanation.surface: With the rum all gone, there is weeping and wailing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hence' is an unusual anagram signal: NO RUM rearranged makes the word for grieve.
explanation.definitionFit: To lament is to grieve aloud over a loss.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'A piece of clastic (4)': the letters are a hidden run in 'clastic', but no clue word defines the answer, so no definition can be given.
Clue held as 'Possibly (5)': the clue is cut short; one word cannot define or build the answer, and no scan or reprint supplies the rest.

parts.note: placed after the 3-letter answer at 10-across, this light completes a word meaning inborn or natural

explanation.surface: Something that is perfectly natural once ten o'clock has passed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After 10' looks like a time of day; it means after the entry at 10-across, a word for a pub, which together make a word meaning inborn.
explanation.definitionFit: Following the word for a pub, these letters make a word for inborn, which is what natural means here.

clue.text: Not a book to read at one sitting

definitions.text: Not a book to read at one sitting

parts.words: Not a book to read at one sitting
parts.note: F. W. Farrar's Victorian school novel is subtitled 'Little by Little', so it is read bit by bit, not in one go

explanation.surface: Advice that a certain long book should not be finished in one session.
explanation.walkthrough: Farrar's 1858 school story is titled 'Eric, or, Little by Little'; the subtitle suggests reading it a little at a time.
explanation.definitionFit: Farrar's moral school story carries the subtitle 'Little by Little', so its title hero names it.

clue.text: You won' get any change out of this (two words)

definitions.text: You won' get any change out of this

parts.words: You won' get any change out of this
parts.note: a railway coach that runs right to the destination means the passenger need not switch trains

explanation.surface: A warning that a purchase will leave you with no money back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' looks like coins given back; it means changing trains, which a coach going all the way avoids.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway coach detached and attached to other trains carries passengers to their destination without switching.

clue.text: Where the wires are pulled (three words)

parts.note: puppets and stage effects are worked by wires from out of the audience's sight, and influence is exerted in secret

explanation.surface: The place where strings are pulled to control events.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wires are pulled' suggests secret influence; it also describes stage machinery worked out of sight in a theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Secret influence and stage machinery both operate out of public view, in the hidden part of a theatre.
